fragments.text: Hello, welcome to my presentation at the Artificial Intelligence for Information Accessibility Conference. My name is Okambolo. I'm a professor in the measurement, evaluation, and data science program at the University of Alberta, Canada. In this presentation, I will be talking about the evolution of assessment literacy in the era of AI, and why assessment literacy should be considered a pillar of AI literacy in higher education. Over the last few years, many genetic AI tools have become accessible, such as Open Apps, JetGPT, Google's Gemini, and Mata's Lama. These tools are capable of generating text, images, audios, and videos based on some user prompts. The increased availability and accessibility of these tools have influenced many fields

including higher education. The Digital Council, Education Council conducted a comprehensive survey back in 2024 with around 4,000 responses from undergraduate and graduate students across 16 countries. The results of this survey offer a diverse range of student viewpoints on AI in education. For instance, 86% of the students reported using AI in their daily studies, and approximately 54% of the students use genetic AI tools at least once a week. These findings suggest that students have already incorporated AI into their learning processes. Also, most students just reported using genetic AI for searching for information as if they were searching for information in a search engine such as Google. Students also reported other use cases of AI such as checking grammar, summarizing documents

such as course notes, paraphrasing documents, and finally creating a first draft for their course assignments such as essays. So while students seem to enjoy genetic AI tools, what is happening on the other side of the table, university instructors? So we know that AI has already created a digital divide in higher education. Digital divide often refers to the gap between individuals with access to and effective use of modern technologies such as internet and computers, and those without. However, even with access, a lack of digital skills or literacy can prevent people from effectively using technology and participating in the digital age. The rise of tools such as GPT has created a great divide among university instructors. On one side, we have university instructors who have proactively adopted AI.

They see AI as a new and powerful tool for teaching and learning. These instructors are already defining creative ways to incorporate it into their courses and they are rethinking their assessments or assignments to leverage the AI's capabilities. On the other side, we have some other instructors who are struggling. So these instructors feel like they just caught off guard, they are overwhelmed by the rapid changes, and they are just trying to figure out how to respond. These instructors are also struggling with how to enforce traditionally academic integrity policies in a world where students have access to such powerful tools. That's why I described this situation as a great divide, a canyon of understanding that

separates these two groups of instructors. Now the challenge before us is to build a bridge across this canyon. Recent surveys administered to university instructors reveal that most instructors are not necessarily prepared to revise their teaching practices, particularly their assessments. At this stage, comprehensive profession development is a strategic must for building a culture of AI forward pedagogy. In this presentation, I argue that institutional strategies, including profession development activities, should combine the concepts of AI and assessment to help educators build assessment and AI literacy. Speaking of assessment and AI literacy, let's just discuss this concept first. Assessment literacy refers to knowledge, skills, and processes associated with designing, selecting, implementing, scoring, and using high-quality assessments to improve student

learning. An assessment literate educator begins any assessment process with a clear purpose and defined learning targets. These educators understand that the quality of assessment directly impacts the dependability of the evidence scattered and the sounds of any decisions that they can just make based on that evidence. On the other hand, AI literacy refers to the knowledge and skills that enable humans to critically understand, evaluate, and use AI systems and tools to safely and ethically participate. AI literacy for faculty extends far beyond just mere proficiency in using tool-such LGBT. It's a comprehensive set of competencies that enable educators to understand, apply, and ethically guide AI in their profession roles, including teaching, research, and administrative duties.

Educators like myself must understand the core principles of AI, use AI tools proficiently, and most importantly, they must be able to integrate AI tools into their teaching practices. So here I argue that AI should be seen as a catalyst for assessment design. Assessment must be AI resilient, rather than AI proof. Assessment must be process-oriented rather than only evaluating the final outcome in our evaluating student learning. And lastly, assessments must utilize AI to cultivate critical thinking rather than merely measuring student's knowledge. Instead of banning AI technologies, instructors should redesign their assessments to test students with critically evaluating the quality, reliability, and bias of AI generated content. So this will just force students to verify information by cross-referencing with credible

sources and applying their own independent judgment which is a core competency of AI literacy. So when charity AI tools first became available, the initial reaction from most educators mostly focused on detecting AI driven cheating and plagiarism, which turned out to be an ineffective approach. A more powerful and sustainable approach is to shift our focus from blocking the technologies to redesigning pedagogical practices. This involves embedding deep assessment literacy within AI training for instructors. Here the goal is to move beyond just asking, how do I catch students using AI, to how do I design assessments that challenge students to demonstrate skills that AI cannot necessarily replicate? By mapping AI capabilities into existing learning objectives, we can first identify the

vulnerabilities of our assignments and assessments. Then we can develop some AI-resistant assessments that can focus on the process, authenticity, and human skills. So rather than using AI detectors to identify cheating and plagiarism, we can use a rubric for example that can reward critical thinking. And lastly, we must use AI-specific, assignment-specific AI policies that can ensure and promote academic integrity. So we already know that take-home essays, un-procative exams, and tradition research papers can be easily completed using AI. So that's why they are not necessarily very effective. Although there are still some assessment options such as in-class exams and proctor digital tests that are less vulnerable to genitive AI, our assessment practices must move away

from this traditionally purchased to more innovative assessments. These tools, or our assessments, can evaluate authentic human skills that cannot be replicated or fake by AI tools. So as I conclude my presentation, I would like to re-inversize that assessment literacy should be a pillar of AI literacy. Integration of assessment literacy within AI literacy is a necessary and durable evolution of today's pedagogical practices. The future of assessment is not about AI replacing instructors like myself, but it's more about a collaborative human-centered model where AI serves as a powerful but carefully-managed partner in the pedagogical process. By grounding the use of AI in the principles of assessment literacy, instructors can harness its potential to create more engaging, authentic, and equitable learning experiences for all learners. So thank you for listening to my presentation and please feel free to contact me with your about your questions or your comments. Goodbye for now.
